entities.summary:
Jean-Baptiste Louis Andrault, marquis de Maulévrier (1677-1754), emerged as a pivotal figure in French military and diplomatic circles during the reigns of Louis XIV and Louis XV, embodying the strategic ambitions of the Bourbon monarchy in early 18th-century Western Europe. His career, spanning the turbulent decades marked by the War of the Spanish Succession and its geopolitical aftermath, saw him rise from a distinguished military engineer to a Marshal of France and a key ambassador, directly influencing French foreign policy and military doctrine across Spain, Italy, and the Low Countries. His work was instrumental in reinforcing the Bourbon dynastic claims and projecting French power through a combination of battlefield expertise and shrewd negotiation.

Andrault de Maulévrier's early military prowess was honed during the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714), where his expertise in siege warfare was particularly noted at the sieges of Lille (1708) and Douai (1710), earning him rapid promotions. Following the conflict, he transitioned to diplomacy, serving as Ambassador to Spain from 1720 to 1724, where he played a crucial role in solidifying the Franco-Spanish alliance under Philip V and Louis XV through the Treaty of Madrid (1721). His later diplomatic posting as Ambassador to Venice (1733-1738) coincided with the War of the Polish Succession, during which he skillfully navigated the complex Italian political landscape to secure French interests and support for the Bourbon cause.
